messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 49

# The Watchman

Marcus has worked security for nearly forty-five years. He's the kind of man who notices things—a shift in someone's gait, the weight distribution of a bag, the way eyes move across a room. This attentiveness has always been his strength, the thing that made him good at his job. At seventy-one, he still walks his rounds at the downtown office complex with the same deliberate pace he's maintained for decades, clipboard in hand, uniform pressed.

On March 14th of last year, Marcus was in the lobby of the building during the evening shift when three men entered through the main entrance. He remembers the precise moment he registered that something was wrong—not from any single detail, but from the absence of the usual details. No briefcases. No ID badges. No purpose in their movement. He was moving toward them when the first explosion came from the parking garage below. The blast lifted him off his feet and threw him against the marble wall. His ears rang with a sound he'd never heard before and has never stopped hearing since.

He remembers fragments: the smell of smoke, the taste of blood in his mouth, someone screaming his name. He remembers crawling toward the security desk, his left shoulder not responding the way it should. The subsequent explosions feel dreamlike now, though the news reports confirm there were two more. Seventeen people died that day. Marcus was one of the thirty-two injured.

His physical wounds healed within months. The shoulder required surgery and physical therapy, but he regained most of his mobility. His wife, Patricia, was relieved when he was cleared to return to work after six months. "You need your routine," she'd said gently. Marcus agreed. Routine had always been his anchor.

But something fundamental has shifted in how his mind works.

Now, when Marcus walks his rounds, his hypervigilance has become something else entirely—something that exhausts rather than protects. Every shadow in a stairwell triggers a cascade of images: the lobby, the dust, the blood on the marble. His hands shake as he checks doors. He's begun conducting his rounds twice, then three times per shift, unable to trust that he actually locked something the first time. Patricia finds him awake at 3 a.m., standing at the window, watching the street below.

The worst part is that his mind no longer trusts the very skill that defined him. When he notices something unusual now—a forgotten package, an unfamiliar face—instead of feeling the calm competence he once felt, he experiences a crushing wave of dread. His heart races. His breathing becomes shallow. He's called the police four times in the past eight months, each time finding nothing. Each time, the shame compounds.

Marcus has stopped going to the grocery store. Patricia does the shopping now. He avoids crowds, which is difficult in a job that requires him to move through public spaces. He's called in sick more times in the past year than in his entire career. When he does go to work, he changes his routine constantly, unable to settle into the patterns that once comforted him. He tells himself this unpredictability keeps him safer, but he knows it's irrational. The knowing doesn't help.

At night, he lies beside Patricia, feeling her breath, grateful she's there. But he's also waiting—always waiting for the next thing to go wrong. His mind has decided the world is fundamentally unsafe, and despite everything he knows intellectually about probability and statistics, he cannot seem to convince himself otherwise.
